ECE 6390 / Navigation

Code correlation

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how a receiver searches for a delayed code within noise.

A receiver tests alignments between the incoming samples rᵢ and a known local code cᵢ. A correlation such as R(d) = (1/N)Σrᵢcᵢ₋d is strongest when their code features align.

At chip rate Rchip, one chip represents a travel-distance interval c/Rchip. Correlation peak shape, signal-to-noise ratio, and integration affect how accurately a delay can be estimated within that interval.

A repeating code identifies delay modulo its period. Absolute timing, code-epoch information, and receiver clock estimation are still needed for an unambiguous navigation measurement. The displayed 15-chip sequence is a teaching code.

Example

At 1 Mchip/s, one chip lasts 1 μs and corresponds to about 300 m of travel distance. A two-chip delay is about 600 m modulo the repeated code period.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. For a repeating 15-chip code, why do delays of 2 and 17 chips produce the same cyclic alignment?

    Compare the delays modulo the code length.

    They differ by exactly one 15-chip period. Cyclic correlation alone identifies both as a two-chip shift; extra timing information is required to distinguish them.
